hero.headline: House votes to end Iran war in bipartisan rebuke to Trump
hero.body:
The House of Representatives passed a war powers resolution on Wednesday directing President Trump to end military hostilities with Iran, marking a rare bipartisan rebuke to the administration. The measure passed 215-208, with four Republicans joining Democrats in support.

The four Republicans who broke ranks were Thomas Massie of Kentucky, Brian Fitzpatrick of Pennsylvania, Warren Davidson of Ohio, and Tom Barrett of Michigan. The vote represented the first success after three previous attempts to pass similar legislation had failed.

War powers resolutions allow Congress to direct the withdrawal of U.S. armed forces from hostilities abroad without requiring presidential approval, though presidents have historically challenged their constitutional authority. The passage of this resolution signals growing unease among lawmakers about the scope and duration of military engagement with Iran.

Despite the symbolic victory for congressional oversight, the measure faces significant practical obstacles to becoming law. Democrats have been unable to advance a war powers resolution in the Senate, where Republican control has blocked similar efforts. Even if the Senate were to pass the measure, President Trump would likely veto it, making passage unlikely in both chambers.

The House vote capped a series of legislative setbacks for the Trump administration in Congress. The measure asserts Congress's constitutional authority over declarations of war and directs the president to remove U.S. forces from hostilities with Iran. The four Republicans who crossed party lines reflected growing erosion in GOP support for the conflict.

The measure now moves to the Senate, where its fate remains uncertain. Republican leadership has demonstrated little appetite for challenging the president on foreign policy matters, making passage in that chamber unlikely. The House vote nonetheless marks a significant moment in the ongoing debate over executive war powers and congressional authority in matters of military conflict.

The bipartisan nature of the vote, though narrow, highlights rising concerns among lawmakers about the direction of U.S. military policy in the region. The resolution represents an assertion of congressional power at a time when some lawmakers have expressed frustration with executive authority over military decisions.

The passage comes as tensions over executive power have intensified across multiple policy areas. The House vote demonstrates that despite Trump's significant influence over the Republican Party, some members remain willing to challenge the administration on major national security decisions.

While the resolution's path forward in the Senate appears blocked, the House action sends a message about congressional sentiment regarding the Iran conflict. Whether additional pressure will mount for Senate action or whether the measure will ultimately be vetoed remains to be seen, but the vote underscores persistent legislative disagreement over the administration's foreign policy approach.

cards.headline: U.S., Israel, and Lebanon announce conditional ceasefire agreement
cards.body:
Israel and Lebanon have agreed to implement a full ceasefire, contingent on Hezbollah halting attacks and withdrawing its operatives from the area south of the Litani River. The agreement was announced in a joint statement from the United States, Israel, and Lebanon.

Hezbollah has already indicated it would agree to a full ceasefire, but whether the Shia militia will accept the specific terms negotiated by Israel and the Lebanese government remains unclear. The Litani River, located in southern Lebanon, serves as a key geographic marker in the agreement, positioned approximately 18 miles north of the Israeli border.

The conditional nature of the ceasefire places significant responsibility on Hezbollah's compliance. The Lebanese government must ensure the militia withdraws its forces from southern Lebanon, while Israel has conditioned its participation on a complete cessation of attacks from Hezbollah. The United States brokered the agreement between the two nations.

However, the fragile ceasefire has already faced serious tests. Israel conducted a massive strike on Lebanon that killed more than 300 people, drawing widespread international condemnation. Israeli officials claimed the attacks specifically targeted Hezbollah members and command posts, though the strikes hit densely populated residential areas in central Beirut and other civilian centers without warning.

The timing of the strikes raised questions about Israel's commitment to the agreement. Hezbollah stated it had been "notified of a ceasefire" and had been "committed to it since this morning," according to Lebanese political sources. Despite this announcement, Israeli strikes continued, and by Thursday, Hezbollah and Israel were trading heavy fire again.

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said the Israeli strikes violated the ceasefire agreement and would render negotiations meaningless. Senior Iranian officials warned of a response against Israel. The Soufan Center thinktank noted that the scale of Israel's strikes was likely to be viewed as escalatory regardless of ceasefire boundaries.

Some analysts suggested Israel may have been unhappy with the ceasefire negotiations. The Wall Street Journal reported that Israel was informed of the deal only at the last minute and "wasn't happy." This has raised concerns about Washington's ability to manage its relationship with Israel while pursuing de-escalation in the Middle East.

According to security experts, Israel's continued military operations in Lebanon could undermine the ceasefire overall and keep the United States trapped in a conflict it is seeking to exit. The Israeli Defense Forces' own assessment reportedly concludes that disarming or defeating Hezbollah is unrealistic despite the latest invasion and bombing campaign.

The ceasefire represents a potential end to hostilities between Israel and the Iran-backed militia, which operates from southern Lebanon. Whether the agreement takes effect depends on Hezbollah's acceptance of the withdrawal requirement. The joint statement did not specify enforcement mechanisms or timelines for implementation.

cards.headline: Wall Street falls as Middle East fighting drives oil prices higher
cards.teaser: Stock indexes ended lower as tensions between Iran and the United States pushed energy costs up and Treasury yields rose.
cards.body:
The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 600 points as tensions between Iran and the United States escalated. Iranian drones struck Kuwait's main international airport, prompting military exchanges between the two nations. Rising oil prices and increased Treasury yields weighed on equity markets.

The market decline ended the S&P 500's nine-session winning streak. Investors grew concerned about how higher oil prices could fuel inflation and squeeze consumer spending and corporate profits.

cards.headline: Trump moves career federal workers into at-will employment classification
cards.teaser: President Trump signed an executive order reclassifying roughly 8,000 federal policy workers into a new employment category that critics say will function like political appointments.
cards.body:
President Trump signed an executive order reclassifying approximately 8,000 senior federal workers, stripping away their job protections. The affected employees earn up to nearly $200,000 annually and work in roles deemed to influence government policy.

The new classification allows these workers to be fired at will, removing the protections that traditionally shielded career civil servants from arbitrary dismissal. Critics contend the order effectively converts protected positions into roles similar to political appointees, undermining the civil service system.

cards.headline: Trump administration plans tariffs on 59 countries over forced labor
cards.teaser: The White House announced levies of up to 12.5 percent on nations that fail to restrict goods made with forced labor.
cards.body:
The Trump administration plans to impose tariffs between 10 and 12.5 percent on approximately 60 trading partners, including the UK, EU, Canada, Taiwan and Australia. Officials cite these countries' alleged failures to adequately address forced labor in their supply chains.

The move represents a shift in how the administration justifies trade restrictions. By anchoring tariffs to labor standards rather than other economic rationales, officials appear to be using a legal framework designed to withstand court challenges. However, critics argue the forced labor justification masks protectionist motivations. The EU has already objected, stating the tariffs breach the spirit of a trade agreement reached with the US last July.

cards.headline: Trump announces $700 million in federal support for coal industry
cards.teaser: President Trump is set to announce approximately $700 million in federal funding to support coal plants and export facilities using wartime authority.
cards.body:
President Trump plans to use wartime authority under the Defense Prevention Act to allocate $700 million to the coal industry. The funding includes $425 million for 13 existing coal plants, $75 million for an export terminal in California, and $185 million for additional coal-related infrastructure.

The announcement represents a significant federal investment in an energy sector that has declined in recent decades. By invoking the Defense Prevention Act, Trump is framing coal industry support as a matter of national security, allowing the administration to bypass typical appropriations processes.

cards.headline: Trump intervenes in Brazil politics ahead of crucial election
cards.teaser: Trump is preparing to support a right-wing ally in Brazil ahead of an election that will test Latin America's left.
cards.body:
Trump appears ready to support a new right-wing ally in Brazil ahead of a crucial election this year. The intervention represents another instance of the president involving himself in Brazilian politics.

The upcoming election will serve as the biggest test for Latin America's left. Trump's willingness to lend assistance to a conservative candidate follows a pattern of engagement with right-wing movements in the region. The election's outcome could shift the political balance in Latin America's largest country.

hero.headline: Iranian attack on Kuwait airport kills one, injures dozens
hero.teaser: An Iranian attack on Kuwait's main airport killed one person and injured dozens, according to Kuwaiti officials.
hero.body:
Iranian drones struck Kuwait's main airport, killing one person and injuring dozens. The attack forced Kuwait to temporarily shut down the passenger terminal. Iran said the strike was retaliation for earlier U.S. attacks on an Iranian oil tanker and island.

The assault tested a fragile ceasefire between the United States and Iran. The coordinated attack came as negotiations between the two countries continued, raising questions about Iran's commitment to ending hostilities in the region.

cards.headline: Israeli strikes kill nine in Lebanon as Hezbollah fires rockets
cards.teaser: Israeli military operations in Lebanon killed nine people while Hezbollah launched rockets over the border, straining a partial ceasefire.
cards.body:
Israeli strikes killed nine people in Lebanon while Hezbollah launched rockets across the border. The violence tested a partial ceasefire agreement that Israel and the Lebanese armed group reached on Monday, intended to reduce hostilities between the two sides.

Israel has continued its military campaign in southern Lebanon following the deal announced by the US, though it has not struck Beirut under the terms of the agreement. Despite the diplomatic framework, both sides continued exchanging fire.

cards.headline: Trump to impose tariffs on dozens of countries over forced labor claims
cards.teaser: The Trump administration plans to impose tariffs of at least 10 percent on approximately 60 trading partners following forced labor investigations.
cards.body:
Trump plans to impose tariffs between 10% and 12.5% on approximately 60 trading partners, including the UK, Canada, the EU, Taiwan, and Australia, citing forced labor concerns. This move represents his latest effort to revive his signature trade policy.

The EU has already responded critically to the proposal, stating it expected the US to honor the tariff deal reached in July and asserting that these new duties violate the agreement's spirit. The tariff announcement comes after the US Supreme Court struck down many of Trump's previous tariffs in February.

cards.headline: Protests grow in Albania over Kushner-linked resort project
cards.teaser: Demonstrations are expanding in Albania against a resort development on Sazan Island linked to Jared Kushner.
cards.body:
Demonstrations have erupted across Albania opposing a resort development on Sazan Island connected to Jared Kushner. The movement, dubbed the "flamingo revolution," has drawn support from environmental and political groups concerned about the project's impact on the island.

The protests reflect growing public resistance to the development plans, with increasing numbers of Albanians joining the opposition campaign against the Kushner-linked resort proposal.

cards.headline: Portugal and Austria win UN Security Council seats, Germany loses bid
cards.teaser: Portugal and Austria defeated Germany in voting for seats on the UN Security Council, marking a diplomatic setback.
cards.body:
Portugal and Austria have won election to the UN Security Council, with Kyrgyzstan also securing a seat for the first time. Germany failed in its bid to win one of the rotating positions on the 15-member body.

The five elected countries will gain temporary influence over international security decisions. Germany's defeat marked an unexpected outcome in the competition for these coveted rotating seats.

cards.headline: Trump intervenes in Brazil politics ahead of crucial election
cards.teaser: Trump is preparing to support a right-wing ally in Brazil ahead of an election that will test Latin America's left.
cards.body:
Trump appears ready to support a new right-wing ally in Brazil ahead of a crucial election this year. The intervention represents another instance of the president involving himself in Brazilian politics.

The upcoming election will serve as the biggest test for Latin America's left. Trump's willingness to lend assistance to a conservative candidate follows a pattern of engagement with right-wing movements in the region. The election's outcome could shift the political balance in Latin America's largest country.

cards.headline: Phone call between Trump and Netanyahu described as difficult
cards.teaser: Reports describe a contentious phone conversation between Trump and Netanyahu, though Israel's leader dismissed friction claims.
cards.body:
President Trump confirmed he called Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu "crazy" during a heated phone call. Trump acknowledged cursing at Netanyahu during the exchange, in which he told the Israeli leader not to bomb the Lebanese capital Beirut.

Netanyahu dismissed reports of friction between the two leaders, but the contentious call has complicated ongoing Iran negotiations. Netanyahu has a history of testing the patience of American presidents.

cards.headline: California governor's race remains unsettled as votes continue to be counted
cards.teaser: Multiple candidates are competing to advance to the general election in California's primary, with the outcome still unclear.
cards.body:
California's gubernatorial primary remained unsettled as election officials continued counting votes. With nearly 60% of ballots tabulated, Republican Steve Hilton held a narrow lead, followed by Democrat Xavier Becerra in second place. Billionaire progressive Tom Steyer trailed in third position.

Under California's top-two primary system, the two candidates with the most votes advance to the general election regardless of party affiliation. The close margins meant final results would depend on outstanding ballots yet to be counted across the state.

cards.headline: Federal judge blocks Trump administration from dismantling weather research center
cards.teaser: A court ruling halted efforts to shut down a climate research facility, but advocates say significant damage has already occurred.
cards.body:
A federal judge blocked the Trump administration from dismantling the National Center for Atmospheric Research. The court cited evidence of political retaliation against Colorado in its decision. Science advocates celebrated the ruling as a victory, though they warned that the administration's actions had already caused harm to the research center's operations.

The dispute centered on the administration's attempt to remove a supercomputer from the climate research facility. The judge's order prevents federal officials from proceeding with plans to dismantle the Boulder-based weather laboratory. The case highlighted tensions between the administration and scientific institutions conducting climate and weather research.

cards.headline: USDA investigating possible flesh-eating screwworm case in South Texas
cards.teaser: Agriculture officials are examining a suspected infection near the U.S.-Mexico border, where the pest was recently detected.
cards.body:
The U.S. Department of Agriculture announced it is investigating a possible case of New World screwworm infection in South Texas. The suspected case emerged after the flesh-eating pest was detected 25 miles from the U.S. border. Texas lawmakers expressed alarm about the proximity of the parasite to American territory.

Screwworms are parasites that infest wounds of warm-blooded animals, including humans and livestock. The pest had been eradicated from the United States in the 1960s through an intensive program. The potential reappearance near the border raised concerns among agricultural officials and public health authorities about the risk of reintroduction.

cards.headline: Senate Republicans begin debate on ICE funding package
cards.teaser: The Senate voted along party lines to consider legislation that would fund immigration enforcement through the end of Trump's term.
cards.body:
The Senate voted along party lines to begin debate on a Republican bill funding immigration enforcement through the end of President Trump's term. Republicans supported the procedural vote while Democrats opposed it.

The legislation would authorize $70 billion in spending for agencies involved in the administration's mass deportation campaign. Senate Republicans initially attempted to include $1 billion for security improvements at a Trump White House ballroom within the measure, but dropped those plans after recognizing the addition could jeopardize passage of the broader immigration enforcement funding.

cards.headline: Democratic challenger selected to face Rep. Tom Kean Jr., who has been absent from public view
cards.teaser: A Democratic nominee has emerged to challenge the Republican congressman, who has been missing from public appearances amid health questions.
cards.body:
Democrats selected a challenger to face Rep. Tom Kean Jr. in the general election. The Republican congressman won his primary despite having vanished from public view for months, prompting questions about his health and whereabouts. Trump had endorsed Kean in the race.

Kean said he would return to work in person within weeks after his extended absence. The congressman's mysterious disappearance from public life became a subject of media scrutiny and constituent concern. For now, the Democratic nominee has the race to herself as attention focuses on when and whether Kean will resume normal congressional activities.

cards.headline: Countries in South China Sea create land to match China's island-building
cards.teaser: After years of watching China expand its territorial claims through artificial islands, other nations are adopting similar tactics.
cards.body:
Countries in the South China Sea have begun creating artificial land formations to support their territorial claims, mirroring China's strategy from previous years. The shift represents a new phase in regional competition over the disputed waters, where multiple nations assert overlapping sovereignty.

China spent years building artificial islands to reinforce its expansive claims in the South China Sea. Other countries in the region are now pursuing the same approach, expanding small features into larger land masses. The development reflects a regional mentality of securing territorial gains while the opportunity exists.

hero.headline: SpaceX sets share price at $135 ahead of largest initial public offering
hero.body:
Elon Musk's SpaceX has announced a share price of $135 for its initial public offering, positioning the rocket manufacturer to become the most valuable company ever to go public. The pricing values SpaceX at $1.75 trillion, surpassing Saudi Aramco's 2019 IPO in both total valuation and capital raised.

The company announced the share price earlier than market observers had anticipated. This timing suggests SpaceX is moving quickly to capitalize on current market conditions as it transitions from private to public ownership.

The path to this announcement included multiple revisions to SpaceX's target valuation in recent weeks. Financial analysts tracking the offering noted that SpaceX lowered its initial targets at least twice before settling on the current $135 per share figure. These downward adjustments may reflect broader concerns about stock market conditions and investor appetite for large public offerings.

SpaceX has not disclosed how many shares it plans to sell or what percentage of the company will be offered to public investors. The company is working to attract both institutional and retail investors willing to purchase shares at the announced price.

The decision to access public capital markets comes as SpaceX's operational demands have grown significantly. The company's activities span satellite launches, government contracts, and development of next-generation spacecraft. These expanding operations appear to require more capital than private investment rounds alone can provide.

The IPO represents a major milestone for SpaceX, which has remained privately held since its founding. Going public will mark a significant shift in how the company operates and is governed. The offering is expected to close in the coming weeks, pending market conditions and regulatory approval.

Saudi Aramco's 2019 public debut had previously set the record for largest IPO. That offering raised substantial capital and valued the Saudi oil company at approximately $1.7 trillion. SpaceX's planned IPO would exceed that historic benchmark in both metrics, reflecting the growing value placed on space industry companies and Musk's ventures.

The timing of SpaceX's IPO coincides with increased investor interest in space technology and commercial spaceflight. The company has established itself as a major player in launching satellites, resupplying the International Space Station, and developing reusable rocket technology. Its government contracts provide a stable revenue stream alongside its commercial operations.

The public offering will give SpaceX direct access to capital markets, allowing it to fund future growth and expansion plans. For public investors, the IPO creates an opportunity to own shares in one of the world's most ambitious space exploration companies. The outcome will likely influence how other aerospace and technology companies approach their own public market debuts.

cards.teaser: Stock indexes ended lower as tensions between Iran and the United States pushed energy costs up and Treasury yields rose.
cards.body:

The market decline ended the S&P 500's nine-session winning streak. Investors grew concerned about how higher oil prices could fuel inflation and squeeze consumer spending and corporate profits.

cards.headline: Alphabet raises record $85 billion for Google AI operations
cards.teaser: The tech giant completed the largest capital raise on record through a convertible preferred stock sale to fund artificial intelligence development.
cards.body:
Alphabet completed the largest equity fundraising in corporate history, raising up to $85 billion through a stock sale to fund its artificial intelligence infrastructure investments. The deal includes a $10 billion investment from Berkshire Hathaway, the investment group formerly led by Warren Buffett.

The massive capital raise underscores investor confidence in AI-related investments as technology companies intensify competition in developing large language models and related products. Analysts noted the fundraising surpasses the combined value of the three largest IPOs ever completed.

cards.headline: Broadcom shares fall despite beating sales targets
cards.teaser: The chipmaker reported first quarter revenue above expectations but saw its stock price drop on software weakness and flat AI chip guidance.
cards.body:
Broadcom exceeded its first quarter sales targets but saw its stock price decline as investors reacted to weak software performance and an unchanged forecast for AI chip sales. The company's stock fell despite reporting revenue growth, driven by concerns about its software division. The AI chip outlook for the full year remained at previous levels rather than showing an increase.

The stock movement reflects investor focus on Broadcom's artificial intelligence chip business, which has been a key driver of growth expectations. Software sales came in below analyst projections, offsetting stronger performance in the company's semiconductor operations.

cards.headline: Trump administration resists court order on tariff refunds
cards.teaser: The White House has begun repaying some tariff money following a court ruling but signaled it may limit how much certain businesses can claim.
cards.body:
The Trump administration has begun processing tariff refunds following a court order but signaled it may limit the amounts certain companies can recover. This partial compliance indicates the administration's reluctance to fully comply with judicial mandates regarding tariff payments collected under previous trade policies.

The refunds stem from cases where tariffs were later deemed improper. The administration's approach to restricting full repayment is likely to trigger additional legal challenges from importers and trade groups seeking to recover the full amounts owed.

cards.headline: Amazon schedules Prime Day for June 23-26
cards.teaser: The retailer moved its annual sales event to June and extended it to four days as shoppers face inflation pressures.
cards.body:
Amazon announced Prime Day will run June 23-26, 2026, maintaining the four-day format while shifting to an earlier month. The company is offering early deals for Prime members ahead of the official start date. The timing reflects consumer concerns about elevated prices across product categories.

The extended sales period allows Amazon to capitalize on a key revenue window. Prime Day remains exclusive to Prime subscribers, a defining feature since the promotion began. Amazon is also introducing AI-generated product images in search results to help guide customers toward relevant items.

hero.headline: NASA declares Mars orbiter MAVEN mission ended after months of silence
hero.body:
NASA has officially concluded the MAVEN mission after losing contact with the spacecraft more than six months ago. The Mars Atmosphere and Volatile Evolution orbiter stopped communicating with ground stations over a weekend and engineers were unable to restore the connection.

The spacecraft went silent after completing a normal orbit behind Mars. All systems appeared to be functioning properly before it passed behind the planet, according to NASA. When MAVEN reappeared from behind Mars, ground control received no signal. The spacecraft and operations teams investigated the anomaly, but communication could not be reestablished.

MAVEN launched in 2013 and reached Mars orbit in 2014, beginning its study of the upper Martian atmosphere and its interaction with solar wind. Over more than a decade of operation, the orbiter collected crucial data about how Mars transformed from a potentially habitable world into the cold, dry planet it is today. Scientists determined that solar wind stripped away most of the Martian atmosphere over billions of years, carrying it into space and changing the planet's climate.

Beyond its primary research mission, MAVEN served an important support function for NASA's surface exploration efforts. The orbiter acted as a communication relay for the Curiosity and Perseverance rovers, helping transmit data from these exploration vehicles back to Earth.

NASA hosted a media call to announce the official end of the mission. The agency acknowledged the emotional impact of losing a spacecraft that had operated so long and contributed so much to Mars science. Scientists described the loss in personal terms, comparing it to losing a loved one.

The loss of MAVEN represents the end of one of NASA's most productive Mars missions. The research conducted by the orbiter provided essential insights into atmospheric loss processes that occur on planets throughout the solar system. Understanding how Mars lost its atmosphere has broader implications for studying planetary climates and the conditions necessary for habitability.

Despite the loss of MAVEN, NASA maintains an active presence at Mars. Two other spacecraft continue to operate in Mars orbit: the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter, which launched in 2005, and Mars Odyssey, which launched in 2001. These missions continue gathering data about the red planet and supporting surface operations.

NASA has not announced plans for a direct replacement for MAVEN. However, the agency remains committed to studying the Martian atmosphere and climate history through future missions. The data already collected by MAVEN will continue to inform scientists' understanding of how planets lose their atmospheres and the solar wind's role in shaping planetary environments.

cards.headline: Alphabet raises record $85 billion for Google AI business expansion
cards.teaser: The parent company of Google sold stock to fund artificial intelligence development, signaling strong investor appetite for AI offerings.
cards.body:
Alphabet conducted the largest equity fundraising ever, raising up to $80 billion through a stock sale to fund Google's artificial intelligence infrastructure investments. The offering includes a $10 billion investment from Berkshire Hathaway, the investment group previously led by Warren Buffett.

The record capital raise surpasses the combined proceeds of the three largest IPOs ever. The fundraising demonstrates strong investor appetite for AI-related offerings, with markets taking note of Alphabet's commitment to funding its vast artificial intelligence expansion.

cards.headline: Possible flesh-eating screwworm infection found in South Texas
cards.teaser: The USDA detected what could be the first breach of the US-Mexico border by the parasitic fly.
cards.body:
The US Department of Agriculture reported a possible screwworm infection in South Texas. If laboratory tests confirm the finding, it would represent the first time the flesh-eating fly has crossed the US-Mexico border.

Screwworms are parasitic flies whose larvae feed on living tissue. The species was eliminated from the United States decades ago but remains present in parts of Central and South America. Confirmation of the infection would trigger containment and eradication protocols.

cards.headline: UK regulator orders Google to change AI search results display
cards.teaser: Google must add clearer source links in AI Overviews and allow British publishers to opt out of the feature.
cards.body:
Britain's Competition and Markets Authority has required Google to modify its AI Overviews feature in response to publisher concerns. The watchdog ordered the company to include more prominent links to source material and allow publishers to opt out of having their content used in AI-generated search summaries.

The CMA said the opt-out requirement would strengthen publishers' negotiating positions with Google. Publishers had complained about reduced click-through traffic and revenue as users increasingly rely on AI summaries rather than visiting original articles.

cards.headline: Roblox acquires AI video company Morpheus to advance Reality Vision project
cards.teaser: The gaming platform bought an artificial intelligence lab that specializes in video world modeling as part of its Roblox Reality initiative.
cards.body:
Roblox has acquired Morpheus AI, a video world model laboratory, to advance its Reality Vision project. The acquisition brings together pioneering AI founders to accelerate the integration of advanced AI-generated content into Roblox's gaming platform.

The Morpheus team will help Roblox expand the types of content creators can build. The technology will be used to generate machines and creatures for games on the platform, enhancing creative possibilities for developers.

cards.headline: Lovable expands Google Cloud partnership with fivefold usage increase
cards.teaser: The multiyear agreement includes expanded access to Anthropic Claude models alongside increased cloud computing resources.
cards.body:
Lovable and Google Cloud have expanded their partnership through a new multiyear agreement that scales Lovable's cloud usage fivefold. The deal also grants Lovable broader access to Anthropic's Claude AI models via Google's platform.

The expansion underscores the increasing demand for AI infrastructure as technology companies scale their operations and capabilities.

cards.headline: Uber plans to deploy 500 data collection vehicles in 2025
cards.teaser: Modified Ioniq 5 vehicles loaded with sensors will gather information for the company's new autonomous vehicle division.
cards.body:
Uber will put 500 sensor-equipped vehicles on roads this year to collect data for AV Labs, its new autonomous vehicle research division. The company plans to use modified Hyundai Ioniq 5 vehicles outfitted with cameras, lidar, and other sensing equipment.

The data collection effort supports Uber's renewed push into self-driving technology. The fleet will capture road conditions, traffic patterns, and other information needed to develop autonomous driving systems.

hero.headline: Russell Wilson retires from NFL, joins CBS Sports
hero.body:
Quarterback Russell Wilson announced his retirement from the NFL after accepting a position with CBS Sports. Wilson, who won a Super Bowl with the Seattle Seahawks, released a video confirming his decision to step away from playing and transition to broadcasting.

The retirement brings an end to a career that saw Wilson establish himself as one of the league's most successful quarterbacks. He led the Seahawks to a Super Bowl victory and became known for his dual-threat abilities and leadership on the field. Wilson's playing career included stints with multiple teams, though he achieved his greatest success in Seattle.

Aaron Glenn, speaking about the quarterback position, acknowledged Wilson's new career path and indicated his team is evaluating options at the position. The departure creates another opening at quarterback across the league as teams finalize their rosters.

Wilson's move to CBS Sports represents a growing trend of prominent players transitioning directly from the field to broadcasting roles. The network secured Wilson's services as he chose to pursue a television career rather than continue playing. NFL Network reported that Wilson accepted the CBS offer, effectively pausing his playing career.

The decision marks a significant shift in the broadcasting landscape as networks compete to add recognizable former players to their coverage teams. Wilson joins a roster of retired NFL stars who have moved into media roles, bringing firsthand experience and name recognition to game analysis and commentary. His Super Bowl victory and years of high-level quarterback play position him as a credible voice for discussing the modern game.

cards.headline: Arrest warrant issued for 49ers receiver Brandon Aiyuk on speeding charge
cards.teaser: Santa Clara County issued an arrest warrant for San Francisco 49ers wide receiver Brandon Aiyuk in connection with a misdemeanor speeding charge.
cards.body:
The warrant stems from a traffic infraction near Levi's Stadium that gained attention after a video showing the speeding incident circulated online. Aiyuk faces a misdemeanor charge related to the traffic violation.

The legal issue adds uncertainty to Aiyuk's situation with the 49ers. The wide receiver is a key offensive player for San Francisco, and the warrant comes as the team prepares for the upcoming season.

cards.headline: Liverpool defender Ibrahima Konate says he battled depression after deaths of teammate and father
cards.teaser: Liverpool defender Ibrahima Konate revealed he struggled with depression during his final season at the club following the deaths of teammate Diogo Jota and his father.
cards.body:
Liverpool defender Ibrahima Konate has opened up about struggling with depression following two significant losses. Teammate Diogo Jota and his own father both died, leaving the player to cope with grief during what turned out to be his final season at the club.

By speaking publicly about his mental health challenges, Konate has drawn attention to the personal difficulties athletes experience away from the pitch. His willingness to discuss depression underscores how grief and loss can deeply affect professional footballers, highlighting the importance of mental health awareness in sport.

cards.headline: Padres cut outfielder Nick Castellanos after 39 games
cards.teaser: The San Diego Padres designated outfielder Nick Castellanos for assignment, ending his brief stint with the team after 39 games.
cards.body:
Castellanos struggled during his time with San Diego, leading the team to part ways with the veteran outfielder. The Padres called up a player named Taylor to fill the roster spot after designating Castellanos.

Castellanos returned to Philadelphia and told ESPN he has no regrets about his career decisions. The outfielder's departure from San Diego came after the Padres determined the partnership was not working as hoped.

cards.headline: NBA Finals begin with Knicks facing Spurs
cards.teaser: The 2026 NBA Finals tipped off with the New York Knicks playing the San Antonio Spurs, with Game 1 coverage airing on ABC.
cards.body:
The New York Knicks and San Antonio Spurs tip off their championship series at 8:30 p.m. ET at the Frost Bank Center. The matchup pits one of basketball's storied franchises seeking to end a long championship drought against the Spurs and their rising star Victor Wembanyama, who has emerged as the league's brightest young talent.

Expert predictions are split on the series outcome, with analysts highlighting Wembanyama and other key players as potential deciding factors in the title race. The Knicks' return to the Finals marks a significant moment for the franchise and the city of New York.

cards.headline: Nick Saban supports college sports legislation as major conferences oppose bill
cards.teaser: Former Alabama coach Nick Saban voiced support for proposed college sports legislation while the SEC and Big Ten conferences pushed back against the bill.
cards.body:
A bipartisan group of senators is advancing legislation to regulate college sports, with former Alabama coach Nick Saban backing the effort. Saban has called on Congress to establish order in the current college sports landscape, according to reporting from AP News and Politico.

The proposed bill faces pushback from major conferences, including the SEC and Big Ten. Lawmakers supporting the legislation are pressing for swift action, warning that without federal intervention, college sports will continue to face problems. The measure could affect how conferences handle expansion and realignment decisions.

cards.headline: 49ers coach praises Myles Garrett ahead of defensive end's arrival
cards.teaser: San Francisco 49ers offensive line coach called Myles Garrett an all-time great player who will present a good challenge for the team.
cards.body:
The comments came after Garrett was traded in what The Athletic described as a seismic deal that could significantly impact the NFL. The defensive end is joining a new team after the blockbuster trade.

Garrett told reporters he looks forward to rushing the quarterback on obvious passing downs with his new squad. Multiple outlets analyzed how the trade affects the league's power rankings and contender tiers following the deal.

hero.headline: Wim Wenders Withdraws 1975 Film Over Topless Scene Shot When Actress Was 13
hero.body:
German director Wim Wenders has withdrawn his 1975 film Wrong Move from circulation due to a scene showing child actress Nastassja Kinski topless when she was 13 years old. The director announced the decision through a public statement released Wednesday, instructing streaming services, television networks, and distribution partners to stop making the film publicly available.

In his statement, Wenders acknowledged that the young actor should have received better protection during the filming process. The decision marks a significant moment for the acclaimed filmmaker, who is known for directing Paris, Texas and Wings of Desire, among other celebrated works.

The withdrawal removes Wrong Move from all forms of distribution nearly five decades after its initial release. The film will no longer be accessible through theatrical screenings, home video releases, or streaming platforms where it previously appeared.

The decision reflects evolving cultural standards regarding the depiction of minors in cinema. In recent years, conversations within the film industry have intensified around content involving children and the responsibility that filmmakers and rights holders carry when reassessing older works. Similar discussions have emerged regarding other films from previous decades that included scenes now widely considered inappropriate or exploitative.

Kinski, who became a prominent actress during the 1970s and 1980s, was at the beginning of her career when Wrong Move was filmed. She has not made public statements about the withdrawal of the film.

Wenders' decision to voluntarily withdraw the work demonstrates an approach some filmmakers have taken to address problematic content in their own catalogs rather than waiting for external pressure or public controversy to force their hand. The director's foundation will oversee the removal of the film from distribution networks.

The withdrawal of Wrong Move represents one of the more visible examples of a filmmaker taking direct action regarding archival content that raises serious ethical concerns about child protection. As cultural attitudes continue to shift regarding the treatment and representation of minors in entertainment, other filmmakers and studios may face similar decisions about works in their collections.

The film had remained in distribution for nearly 50 years before this withdrawal, suggesting that awareness of the problematic scene may have increased in recent years as discussions around child safety in film production have become more prominent. Wenders' statement indicates a recognition that industry standards have changed significantly since the film's production in the mid-1970s.

cards.headline: Former 60 Minutes Correspondent Says CBS News Under Bari Weiss Is Disastrous
cards.teaser: Steve Kroft called the direction of 60 Minutes under CBS News boss Bari Weiss disastrous following the firing of Scott Pelley and other personnel changes.
cards.body:
Steve Kroft, a veteran 60 Minutes correspondent, criticized the current direction of the program under CBS News leadership in an interview with PBS NewsHour reporter Geoff Bennett. Kroft characterized the changes as journalistic interference, despite 60 Minutes remaining the highest-rated program in its time slot.

His comments follow Scott Pelley's firing from his correspondent position. Pelley had confronted CBS News management in a staff meeting, accusing leadership of "murdering" the show after the network dismissed the executive producer, executive editor, and correspondents Sharyn Alfonsi and Cecilia Vega. Bari Weiss, CBS News editor-in-chief, said Pelley violated standards of "trust and mutual respect."

cards.headline: Bari Weiss Says Fired 60 Minutes Correspondent Scott Pelley Violated Trust
cards.teaser: CBS News boss Bari Weiss stated that fired 60 Minutes correspondent Scott Pelley violated trust and mutual respect, according to reporting by The Washington Post.
cards.body:
Bari Weiss, CBS News editor-in-chief, cited violations of trust and mutual respect in firing Scott Pelley from his correspondent role at 60 Minutes. Pelley had been a longtime fixture on the program before his termination as part of a broader overhaul that also removed the show's executive producer, executive editor, and correspondent Sharyn Alfonsi and Cecilia Vega.

Pelley responded publicly, accusing CBS executives of instructing him to "inject falsehoods and bias" into his reporting and of silencing employees. He defended 60 Minutes' decades-long success, stating the show's audience values integrity and quality. The firings have drawn sharp criticism from industry veterans, including former correspondent Steve Kroft, who called the network's direction "disastrous" under the new leadership.

cards.headline: Charli D'Amelio Cuts Ties With Family Company Amid Financial Dispute
cards.teaser: Social media star Charli D'Amelio has separated from her family's company following reports that almost eight figures went missing from her accounts.
cards.body:
Charli D'Amelio ended her business relationship with her family's company as financial questions emerged about her accounts. The TikTok star stated that almost eight figures had gone missing from her accounts, prompting her family to search for answers. D'Amelio posted a cryptic TikTok saying she was depressed amid the situation.

Her father responded to speculation about a family feud, claiming that his daughter was being manipulated. The financial dispute has generated significant attention given D'Amelio's status as one of social media's highest-earning personalities. The separation from the family company represents a major shift in how D'Amelio manages her business interests.

cards.headline: Tom Holland Explains Previous Comments About Playing Spider-Man Past 30
cards.teaser: Tom Holland said his 2021 statement about not wanting to play Spider-Man past age 30 may have been a negotiating tactic to create leverage with Sony.
cards.body:
Tom Holland addressed comments he made in 2021 to GQ magazine, when he stated that playing Spider-Man after turning 30 would mean he had done something wrong. The actor, now 30 years old, revealed that the statement may have been a strategy to create fear and leverage a better deal with Sony. He described it as an attempt to strengthen his negotiating position.

Holland's new Spider-Man film, Brand New Day, opens in theaters on July 31. The actor has no immediate plans to stop playing the character despite his previous comments. His admission provides insight into the business negotiations between actors and studios in major franchise deals.

cards.headline: Content Creator Lena the Plug Files for Divorce from Podcaster Adam22
cards.teaser: Content creator Lena the Plug has filed for divorce from her husband, podcaster Adam22, according to court records.
cards.body:
Lena the Plug filed for divorce from Adam22, ending the marriage between the two online personalities. Both have built substantial followings through their respective content creation work, with Adam22 known for his podcast interviews in the music and culture space.

Following news of the divorce filing, Adam22 posted on social media encouraging women to send him direct messages. The split has generated widespread attention among their combined audience. Both creators have been public figures in online entertainment for several years.

cards.headline: NBA Finals Begin With Knicks Facing Spurs for Championship
cards.teaser: The New York Knicks and San Antonio Spurs tip off the NBA Finals championship series, which started on June 3.
cards.body:
The NBA Finals 2026 matchup between the New York Knicks and San Antonio Spurs represents a significant moment for both franchises. The Knicks, who last won a championship in 1973, are seeking to end their long title drought after finishing the regular season with a 53-29 record and advancing through the playoffs.

The series tips off at 8:30pm ET at the Frost Bank Center, with Victor Wembanyama and the young Spurs squad facing the hot Knicks team. The championship series will determine which team hoists the Larry O'Brien Championship Trophy.

hero.headline: U.S., Israel, and Lebanon announce conditional ceasefire agreement
hero.body:
Israel and Lebanon have agreed to implement a full ceasefire, contingent on Hezbollah halting attacks and withdrawing its operatives from the area south of the Litani River. The agreement was announced in a joint statement from the United States, Israel, and Lebanon.

Hezbollah has already indicated it would agree to a full ceasefire, but whether the Shia militia will accept the specific terms negotiated by Israel and the Lebanese government remains unclear. The Litani River, located in southern Lebanon, serves as a key geographic marker in the agreement, positioned approximately 18 miles north of the Israeli border.

The conditional nature of the ceasefire places significant responsibility on Hezbollah's compliance. The Lebanese government must ensure the militia withdraws its forces from southern Lebanon, while Israel has conditioned its participation on a complete cessation of attacks from Hezbollah. The United States brokered the agreement between the two nations.

However, the fragile ceasefire has already faced serious tests. Israel conducted a massive strike on Lebanon that killed more than 300 people, drawing widespread international condemnation. Israeli officials claimed the attacks specifically targeted Hezbollah members and command posts, though the strikes hit densely populated residential areas in central Beirut and other civilian centers without warning.

The timing of the strikes raised questions about Israel's commitment to the agreement. Hezbollah stated it had been "notified of a ceasefire" and had been "committed to it since this morning," according to Lebanese political sources. Despite this announcement, Israeli strikes continued, and by Thursday, Hezbollah and Israel were trading heavy fire again.

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said the Israeli strikes violated the ceasefire agreement and would render negotiations meaningless. Senior Iranian officials warned of a response against Israel. The Soufan Center thinktank noted that the scale of Israel's strikes was likely to be viewed as escalatory regardless of ceasefire boundaries.

Some analysts suggested Israel may have been unhappy with the ceasefire negotiations. The Wall Street Journal reported that Israel was informed of the deal only at the last minute and "wasn't happy." This has raised concerns about Washington's ability to manage its relationship with Israel while pursuing de-escalation in the Middle East.

According to security experts, Israel's continued military operations in Lebanon could undermine the ceasefire overall and keep the United States trapped in a conflict it is seeking to exit. The Israeli Defense Forces' own assessment reportedly concludes that disarming or defeating Hezbollah is unrealistic despite the latest invasion and bombing campaign.

The ceasefire represents a potential end to hostilities between Israel and the Iran-backed militia, which operates from southern Lebanon. Whether the agreement takes effect depends on Hezbollah's acceptance of the withdrawal requirement. The joint statement did not specify enforcement mechanisms or timelines for implementation.

cards.headline: Trump moves career federal workers into at-will employment classification
cards.teaser: President Trump signed an executive order reclassifying roughly 8,000 federal policy workers into a new employment category that critics say will function like political appointments.
cards.body:
President Trump signed an executive order reclassifying approximately 8,000 senior federal workers, stripping away their job protections. The affected employees earn up to nearly $200,000 annually and work in roles deemed to influence government policy.

The new classification allows these workers to be fired at will, removing the protections that traditionally shielded career civil servants from arbitrary dismissal. Critics contend the order effectively converts protected positions into roles similar to political appointees, undermining the civil service system.

cards.headline: Four House Republicans cross party lines on Iran war powers and Ukraine votes
cards.teaser: Several GOP lawmakers joined Democrats to pass a resolution forcing the Trump administration to end military action against Iran and to advance Ukraine support legislation.
cards.body:
Four Republican representatives joined House Democrats to pass a war powers resolution directing the Trump administration to end military operations against Iran. The 215-208 vote marked a rare bipartisan rebuke, though the measure is largely symbolic since it faces an uncertain path in the Senate and would likely face a presidential veto.

The same group of Republicans also voted to advance legislation supporting Ukraine in its conflict with Russia. These votes demonstrate uncommon cross-party agreement on foreign policy matters, with GOP lawmakers breaking ranks on issues of military engagement and international support.

cards.headline: Deb Haaland wins New Mexico Democratic gubernatorial primary
cards.teaser: Former Biden administration official Deb Haaland won the Democratic nomination for New Mexico governor and could become the first female Native American governor if elected.
cards.body:
Deb Haaland, who served in the Biden administration, secured the Democratic nomination in New Mexico's gubernatorial primary. Her victory sets up a general election campaign where she could make history as the first female Native American to serve as a state governor.

Haaland's win represents a significant milestone for Native American political representation at the state executive level. The general election will determine whether she can convert the primary victory into a gubernatorial win in New Mexico.

cards.headline: Steve Hilton and Xavier Becerra lead in California governor primary
cards.teaser: Republican Steve Hilton and Democrat Xavier Becerra are leading their respective parties in the California gubernatorial primary to replace Gov. Gavin Newsom.
cards.body:
Steve Hilton leads among Republican candidates in California's gubernatorial primary, while Xavier Becerra holds an advantage in the Democratic field. The primary will determine the nominees to replace Gov. Gavin Newsom, who is not seeking reelection.

The next California governor will almost certainly be a Democrat. Becerra, the establishment favorite, represents a traditional approach to leadership. The outcome will shape whether the state continues on a path of corporate-friendly liberalism or pursues a different direction under a Democrat like Tom Steyer.

cards.headline: Trump announces $700 million in federal support for coal industry
cards.teaser: President Trump is set to announce approximately $700 million in federal funding to support coal plants and export facilities using wartime authority.
cards.body:
President Trump plans to use wartime authority under the Defense Prevention Act to allocate $700 million to the coal industry. The funding includes $425 million for 13 existing coal plants, $75 million for an export terminal in California, and $185 million for additional coal-related infrastructure.

The announcement represents a significant federal investment in an energy sector that has declined in recent decades. By invoking the Defense Prevention Act, Trump is framing coal industry support as a matter of national security, allowing the administration to bypass typical appropriations processes.

cards.headline: Pentagon faces lawsuit over Stars and Stripes editorial control
cards.teaser: Two advisory board members for the military newspaper Stars and Stripes sued the Pentagon, alleging its reorganization undermines the publication's editorial independence.
cards.body:
Two members of the Stars and Stripes advisory board filed a lawsuit against the Pentagon, challenging the Defense Department's restructuring of the military newspaper. The lawsuit alleges that the department is attempting to exert unprecedented control over the publication's editorial operations.

The suit asks a federal judge to block the Pentagon's efforts, arguing that the changes threaten the newspaper's long-standing editorial independence. Stars and Stripes has historically operated with editorial freedom despite its military affiliation and government funding.
